---

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given that capable AI writing assistants can perform much of the cognitive work an assessment is meant to elicit, undetectably in most current implementations, which assessment format(s) — not necessarily a single one, and not necessarily either of the two named — best support the specific credentialing and learning-feedback inferences each course actually needs to certify, at a resourcing and equity cost the institution can sustain?

**Success criteria:**
1. Section 6's "Recommended approach" names the actual construct(s) each recommended format is meant to certify (not merely "prevent cheating" or "test knowledge") for each course category it distinguishes.
2. Section 6's "Recommended approach" lists more than two named formats or conditions rather than presenting a binary timed-exam-versus-take-home choice.
3. Section 6's "Key insight" states, as its finding, whether the pre-AI timed exam was ever a clean measure of the target construct.
4. Section 6's "Recommended approach" names at least two distinct conditions (construct type, field, resourcing) governing which format applies, rather than a context-free flat yes/no.
5. Section 6's "Trade-offs acknowledged" and "Confidence" lines name at least one second-order effect each on student behavior, equity, faculty workload, or institutional/credential reputation, traceable to a chain carrying `[2nd]`/`[3rd]` order marks in section 4.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

**Fishbone breadth-map (Phase 2 technique, default six-category set):** before classifying individual assumptions, the space of *why an assessment format might fail to measure its target construct* was mapped by category — People (test anxiety distorting timed performance; instructor time constraints preventing authentic redesign), Process (task format mismatched to learning objective; no verification step for authorship), Technology and Tools (AI assistants performing the task undetectably; AI-detection tools carrying differential bias — see GT-2), Environment (exam-hall conditions vs. unequal home environments), Information (construct opacity to students; faculty lacking downstream-performance data), Resources (proctoring infrastructure cost vs. redesign/verification staffing cost, and unequal student access to capable AI tools). Each branch below enters the table as a classified assumption; the fishbone's function was to surface breadth, not to itself verify any branch.

**Inversion (Phase 2 technique):** inverting the claim "switching to take-home assessment improves legitimate learning-measurement outcomes" and enumerating failure-guaranteeing conditions produced the preconditions tagged A-9 through A-13 below — several of them, if false, individually or jointly guarantee the switch fails for a given course.

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-1: The choice is binary — timed-proctored exam OR take-home assessment | Convention (framing artifact) | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — the framing collapses the option space; four-plus viable formats survive knockout screening in chain C1 | unverified — flagged, discarded before use in any chain |
| A-2: AI-assisted writing is inherently illegitimate for assessment purposes | Convention | Explicitly challenge | Challenge — legitimacy is context-dependent on the construct being certified (GT-5?, GT-8), not a fixed property of AI assistance itself | unverified — flagged, resolved via chains C1/C3/C4 |
| A-3: Pre-AI timed exams were a clean measure of the target construct (AI is the first thing to compromise their validity) | Untested belief | Verify or flag | Discard — contradicted by GT-1 (construct-irrelevant variance from speededness/stress predates AI) | GT-1, read-at-source; chain C4 |
| A-4: AI-detection software / proctoring is the only lever available to preserve assessment integrity | Convention | Explicitly challenge | Discard — task redesign (authenticity), verification steps (oral defense, process-tracking), and construct redefinition are independent, non-detection levers (chains C1, C3) | unverified — flagged, discarded via trade-off options C/D/E |
| A-5: A single university-wide blanket policy is the appropriate unit of decision | Untested belief | Verify or flag | Discard as default — chain C1's recommendation is construct-specific, not blanket, though administrative pressure toward blanket policy is itself a named risk (pre-mortem Cluster 1) | unverified — flagged |
| A-6: AI capability/availability is stable enough that a policy fixed today remains valid indefinitely | Current constraint | Record expiry conditions | Accept — expires whenever a materially more- or less-capable/detectable class of AI tool becomes available; requires fixed-cadence (e.g., annual) policy review, not set-and-forget | unverified — flagged as a standing expiry condition on the whole recommendation |
| A-7: Take-home formats are categorically more valid than timed exams for "deep understanding" | Convention (embedded in the prompt's own pro-take-home framing) | Explicitly challenge | Challenge — true only for constructs without a hard real-time-performance requirement (GT-5?); false for the identifiable minority of licensure/safety-critical constructs (chain C1's carve-out for option A) | unverified — flagged |
| A-8: The credentialing stakeholder's interest is fully captured by "did the student learn," ignoring third-party signaling | Untested belief | Verify or flag | Discard as a completeness claim — GT-4?/GT-7? show third-party signaling to employers/licensing bodies is a distinct additional interest, exactly what unverifiable take-home formats threaten (chain C3) | unverified — flagged |
| A-9 (from inversion): The downstream task genuinely requires unaided, real-time performance (licensure/safety-critical field) | Current constraint (field-specific fact) | Record expiry — applies only to specific programs | Accept — expires (i.e., does not apply) outside nursing/law/board-licensure/live-interpretation-type programs; drives the option-A carve-out in chain C1 | unverified — flagged |
| A-10 (from inversion): Faculty have, or will be given, adequate time/resources to redesign assessments authentically | Current constraint | Record expiry — becomes true only if the institution allocates a resourcing floor | Challenge — GT-10? indicates this is not currently true at most institutions; pre-mortem Cluster 1 makes resourcing an explicit precondition of rollout, not an aspiration | unverified — flagged |
| A-11 (from inversion): Students face materially unequal access to capable AI tools or skill in using them | Untested belief (plausible, not measured here) | Verify or flag | Challenge — not resolved in this analysis; if true, AI-tolerant take-home formats could widen rather than narrow equity gaps, a genuine open risk (see Abandoned Reasoning) | unverified — flagged, not empirically resolved in this run |
| A-12 (from inversion): No verification structure (oral defense, process trace) accompanies the take-home | Convention (the "naive" default configuration) | Explicitly challenge | Discard as a design default — option C explicitly rejects this configuration by pairing take-home with a verification step | unverified — flagged, discarded in favor of verified designs |
| A-13 (from inversion): Grade inflation / signal collapse leads external stakeholders to distrust the institution's credential | Untested belief (slow-moving, downstream) | Verify or flag | Challenge — not resolved in this analysis; monitored via the external-communication mitigation named in pre-mortem Cluster 3 | unverified — flagged |
| A-14 (audit-surfaced, chain C1 step 1): Default institutional weighting used in the trade-off reflects a "typical" institution's actual stakes ordering | Untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — the flip test in chain C1 shows the D-vs-C ranking is sensitive to a 1-point change in this weighting, so the assumption is explicitly load-bearing, not incidental | unverified — flagged |
| A-15 (audit-surfaced, chain C1 step 4): Course-level learning objectives are, or can be made, explicit enough to assign each course to a construct category | Untested belief | Verify or flag | Challenge — this is a precondition for the entire conditional recommendation to be operationalizable; if false, the "it depends" policy cannot be executed cleanly (pre-mortem Cluster 1) | unverified — flagged |
| A-16 (audit-surfaced, chain C2 step 2): A commercial ed-tech market will respond to institutional policy shifts with new verification/detection tools within a relevant time horizon | Convention / current constraint (market-behavior extrapolation) | Record expiry — market response speed is not guaranteed | Accept — low risk if wrong; does not undermine the core recommendation either way | unverified — flagged |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**Five-Whys reduce-to-primitives (Phase 3 technique) for GT-8:** Claim tested: "A submitted take-home text artifact demonstrates that the named student possesses the capability the course claims to certify." Constituent 1: the work product was produced predominantly by the named student's own cognition — irreducibility check: is this verified by anything intrinsic to the artifact? No; in the absence of a process record (drafts, timestamps, oral defense) this is *assumed*, not observed — Assumed, unverified branch, feeding GT-9?/GT-12(A-12). Constituent 2: the surface form of a well-prepared student's output and a well-prompted AI system's output can converge for open-ended writing prompts — irreducibility check: is this a further-reducible claim or a bottom fact? It bottoms out at a definitional/informational fact about text as a medium — a finished natural-language artifact does not carry its own generation-process metadata unless something external attaches it. This bottom fact is verified by definition (not by citation) and is promoted below as GT-8, unsuffixed. Parent claim verdict: NOT verified as stated (Constituent 1 fails), which is exactly why an unverified take-home artifact cannot alone support the credentialing inference — this finding feeds chain C3.

- **GT-1** Construct-irrelevant variance is a named, recognized threat to assessment validity: systematic score variance from factors unrelated to the intended construct (e.g., language barriers, test speededness, contextual stress that "alienate and confuse" some examinees and "distort task performance" for reasons unrelated to what is being measured) — source: Frontiers in Education (2021), "A Framework of Construct-Irrelevant Variance for Contextualized Constructed Response Assessment," quoting Messick (1989, p.19); read-at-source: quote ("contextual features that engage and motivate one [examinee]...may alienate and confuse another...and bias or distort task performance") located via direct fetch of the Frontiers article. (Note: this reads the Frontiers 2021 secondary presentation of Messick's framework directly; the primary 1989 monograph itself was not independently opened in this run.)
- **GT-2** Commercial AI-text detectors tested on non-native-English TOEFL essays (n=91) versus native-English 8th-grade essays (n=88), across 7 detectors (Originality.AI, Quil.org, Sapling, OpenAI, Crossplag, GPTZero, ZeroGPT), produced an average false-positive rate of 61.22% on non-native essays versus 5.19% on native essays, with 97.80% of non-native essays flagged by at least one detector — source: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, Zou, "GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers," arXiv:2304.02819 (published in *Patterns*, 2023); read-at-source: figures located and quoted directly from arxiv.org/html/2304.02819 via fetch.
- **GT-3?** General-purpose LLMs (the class stipulated in the prompt — Claude, GPT-class systems) can generate fluent, structurally competent, subject-plausible prose in response to most standard undergraduate open-ended writing prompts within seconds, without the requester having independently performed the underlying synthesis — reported-by-delegate: stipulated as a background premise in the user's own prompt/context ("capable AI writing assistants... widely available"), not independently benchmarked against a specific evaluation source in this analysis.
- **GT-4?** A credential (grade or degree) functions as an information signal to third parties (employers, licensing bodies, graduate programs) who did not observe the work being produced and who rely on the institution's certification process to infer the credentialed individual's capability — unverified: general signaling-theory framing (Spence-lineage), no specific source opened in this run.
- **GT-5?** For most post-graduation knowledge-work tasks a degree is meant to prepare a graduate for, the operative real-world performance constraint is "produce a correct/insightful output within a reasonable deadline, with reference tools available," not "produce it unaided within a short, fixed, proctored window"; the reverse (unaided, strict real-time, tool-free) is the binding constraint mainly in an identifiable minority of safety-critical or licensure-gated professions (e.g., emergency medicine triage, courtroom advocacy, licensure board exams, live interpretation) — unverified: professional-practice domain knowledge, no external source opened in this run.
- **GT-6?** Oral examination / viva voce defense and in-person process-tracking (draft-history review, live follow-up questioning on submitted work) are long-standing, pre-AI-era methods institutions have used to verify that a submitted work product reflects the named individual's own understanding — unverified: historical/procedural domain knowledge (e.g., doctoral viva tradition), no external source opened in this run.
- **GT-7?** Aggregate market trust in a credential is a function of perceived reliability of the institution's certification process; a widely-held belief that an institution's assessments cannot verify individual authorship discounts the credential's signaling value for all of that institution's graduates, not only for individuals who obtained undisclosed help — unverified: inference from signaling theory, no external source opened in this run.
- **GT-8** A finished natural-language text artifact, evaluated without any accompanying process record (drafts, timestamps, an oral defense, or in-person work-checks), does not by itself reveal whether it was produced predominantly by the named submitter's own cognition or predominantly by a generative AI system the submitter prompted, because both processes can converge on similar or indistinguishable surface-level output for many open-ended writing tasks — verified by the reduce-to-primitives decomposition above (definitional/informational entailment about text as a medium, not an empirical citation; non-vacuous given GT-3?'s qualitative capability claim).
- **GT-9?** Take-home formats that are "authentic" (requiring inputs — in-class-generated data, personally collected artifacts, student-specific case material — not available to a generic external AI session) and/or paired with a verification step (oral defense, process-tracking) substantially narrow the GT-8 authorship-ambiguity gap, because they either require inputs a generic AI session lacks or add an independent evidentiary channel a purely textual artifact does not have — unverified: inference from GT-6? and general evidence-channel logic; no institutional efficacy data available in this run. This is the single most decision-critical unverified input in the analysis.
- **GT-10?** Redesigning assessments to be authentic and/or verification-paired at scale requires additional faculty/TA time (personalized task design, rubric rework, per-student oral checks) that is a real, current resource constraint at most institutions, particularly at high student-to-faculty ratios — unverified: institutional/practical domain knowledge, no external source opened in this run; current constraint — expires if institutions invest in TA support, AI-assisted grading tools, or restructure section sizes.

**Provenance summary:** `?`-marked: GT-3, GT-4, GT-5, GT-6, GT-7, GT-9, GT-10 (7 of 10). Read-at-source: GT-1 — Frontiers in Education (2021) article, quoted passage citing Messick (1989, p.19) located via direct fetch; GT-2 — arxiv.org/html/2304.02819, false-positive-rate figures (61.22% vs. 5.19%; 97.80% flagged-by-at-least-one-detector) located and quoted via direct fetch. GT-8 is unsuffixed on definitional-entailment grounds (verified by the reduce-to-primitives test above, not by source citation) rather than read-at-source.

---

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Trade-off analysis (Phase 4 technique) — full matrix supporting Conclusion C1

**Options named, including status quo:** (A) Status quo — timed, proctored, closed-book/closed-AI written exam. (B) Naive full switch — unverified take-home, no redesign, no check. (C) Authentic take-home + standardized verification step (oral spot-check or brief follow-up). (D) AI-inclusive timed in-class judgment task (critique/correct/apply an AI-generated draft under time pressure). (E) Portfolio-with-periodic-checks across the term.

**Must-have knockouts (applied before scoring):** (1) must support the credentialing inference the course claims to certify; (2) must be deliverable within real faculty/TA resourcing; (3) must not rely on AI-detector verdicts as the primary integrity mechanism (per GT-2's 61.22%-vs-5.19% disparate false-positive rate). Option B fails knockout (1) for any course making an individual-capability claim (per GT-8/chain C3) and survives only in the narrow carve-out of courses with no such claim (e.g., team deliverables explicitly scored as AI-collaborative output). "Status quo + AI-detector enforcement" (a commonly proposed patch, not one of the five named options) fails knockout (3) outright and is not scored. A, C, D, E survive to scoring for the general case.

**Criteria, weights (1–5, locked before scoring), and anchors:**
1. Construct validity for the claimed target (weight 5): 1 = score mostly explained by factors unrelated to the construct; 5 = score variance overwhelmingly explained by the construct.
2. Resistance to undetectable AI substitution of the credentialed inference (weight 4): 1 = top score achievable with near-zero personal cognitive contribution and no realistic chance of being asked to explain; 5 = substantial AI-only reliance would very likely surface.
3. Equity across student circumstances (weight 4): 1 = strongly disadvantages a group; 5 = roughly equal footing.
4. Faculty/institutional resource feasibility at scale (weight 3): 1 = requires unstaffable per-student time; 5 = deliverable within current typical staffing.
5. Authenticity to post-graduation task conditions, field-relative (weight 3): 1 = performance conditions bear little resemblance to how the relevant work is actually done; 5 = closely mirrors real post-graduation conditions for the specific field.
6. Student stress/wellbeing distortion (weight 2): 1 = high artificial single-sitting stress; 5 = minimal artificial distortion.

**Scores (cited to ground truths) and weighted totals (weight sum = 21):**

| Criterion (weight) | A: status quo | C: authentic+verified | D: AI-inclusive timed | E: portfolio+checks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Construct validity (5) | 3 (GT-1: some CIV present) | 4 (GT-9?) | 4 (targets the AI-era construct directly) | 4 (similar logic to C) |
| AI-substitution resistance (4) | 5 (proctoring blocks live AI use) | 4 (GT-9?: not perfect) | 5 (proctored + task design resists disguise) | 3 (spread across many artifacts, harder to spot-check all) |
| Equity (3→4 col; weight 4) | 2 (GT-1's CIV: speededness/stress) | 4 (avoids GT-2's detector-bias harm; new live-defense stress risk) | 3 (retains GT-1's stress cost; avoids detector-bias risk) | 4 (spreads stakes; avoids detector-bias risk) |
| Resource feasibility (3) | 5 (already resourced/entrenched) | 2 (GT-10?: per-student redesign+check cost) | 3 (one-time redesign, reuses proctoring infra) | 2 (heaviest ongoing grading load) |
| Authenticity, field-relative (3) | 2 (general case; 4–5 for licensure/real-time fields) | 4 (mirrors applied professional work with tools) | 5 (mirrors the emerging AI-judgment task directly) | 4 (mirrors iterative real-world drafting/revision) |
| Wellbeing (2) | 1 (highest single-sitting stress by design) | 3 (removes exam stress, adds live-defense stress) | 1 (same stress profile as A) | 4 (spreads pressure over term) |
| **Weighted total** | **66** | **76** | **78** | **74** |

**Ranking:** D (78) > C (76) > E (74) > A (66). **Flip test:** the smallest single-weight change that changes the winner is raising the wellbeing weight (criterion 6) from 2 to 3 — a move of 1 — which flips the D/C ranking in favor of C; no single-weight move flips A into the lead within the 1–5 range. The D–C gap is therefore a near-tie sensitive to how heavily an institution values student wellbeing relative to construct validity/integrity, while A's last-place standing (for non-real-time-construct courses) is robust to any single-weight change.

### Conclusion C1: The construct-appropriate assessment choice is D for AI-saturated-judgment courses, C (or E where resourcing favors it) for applied-synthesis courses without a real-time requirement, and A only where the target construct is itself unaided real-time performance

GT-1 (construct-irrelevant variance framework) + GT-8 (text artifacts are authorship-process-agnostic) + GT-9? (authentic/verified redesign narrows the authorship gap)
→ scoring the four surviving formats against six weighted criteria anchored in GT-1, GT-2, GT-8, GT-9? and GT-10? produces weighted totals [Assumes: A-14]
→ the totals are A=66, C=76, D=78, E=74 out of a 21-unit weight scale
→ D leads narrowly ahead of C, and both lead clearly ahead of A and E
→ the D-C gap flips under a one-point increase to the wellbeing weight, marking it a near-tie rather than a decisive result
→ no single weight move flips A into the lead within the allowed 1-5 range
→ the status-quo timed-proctored exam is therefore the weakest surviving option for any course whose target construct is applied synthesis or AI-saturated professional judgment
→ the construct-appropriate choice is D where the target construct is judgment-in-context-with-tools [Assumes: A-15]
→ the choice is C, or E where resourcing favors it, where the target construct is applied synthesis without a hard real-time requirement
→ the choice remains A only where the target construct is itself unaided real-time performance

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-8, GT-9? · ?-marked: GT-9? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** LOW — Inputs axis short: GT-9? (the claim that verification/authenticity meaningfully narrows the authorship gap in practice) is unverified against real institutional data; the verification that would remove it is a resourced pilot comparing verified-take-home scores against later-course/downstream performance. Rivals axis also short: option E remains a live, near-tied rival (flip test above) that Abandoned Reasoning does not fully settle — an institution weighting wellbeing more heavily than this analysis's default should prefer E over D for the relevant courses. Inference axis: the weighted-totals hop rests on [Assumes: A-14] (default weighting), whose sensitivity is priced via the flip test above; the construct-assignment hop rests on [Assumes: A-15] (course-objective categorization feasibility), whose failure mode is not priced further here and is carried into the Conclusion's confidence line instead. Two axes short (Inputs, Rivals) caps this chain at LOW regardless of the third.

### Conclusion C2: A construct-differentiated redesign only survives long enough to matter if it is resourced and its redefinition of the credential is actively communicated to external stakeholders — otherwise it drifts back to the status quo or re-imports the harm it was meant to avoid

C1 (construct-appropriate conditional redesign) + GT-10? (redesign resource constraint) + GT-7? (credential signaling depends on external trust)
→[2nd] students reallocate effort toward AI-judgment or defensible-authorship skills once the redesign holds
→[2nd] faculty reallocate effort toward a redesign burden they may under-resource
→[3rd] employers and licensing bodies only recalibrate trust once graduate performance is observed years later
→[3rd] a commercial market for authorship-verification tools emerges in response [Assumes: A-16]
→[3rd] some of those tools reproduce GT-2's detector-bias problem in a new guise, so adopting them reflexively re-imports the equity harm the redesign was meant to avoid
→[3rd] because the credential's certified construct is being redefined internally, its external signaling value depends on employers and licensing bodies being told about the redefinition
→[3rd] a conditional, per-construct policy is administratively harder to sustain than a blanket rule
→[3rd] without an explicit resourcing and communication commitment, the institution is likely to drift back to the status quo out of implementation convenience rather than merit

**Confidence:** LOW — capped by C1's LOW rating (a chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites). Independently: GT-10? (faculty resourcing) is unverified — the verification that would remove it is a budgeted pilot with protected redesign time; GT-7? (market-trust discount mechanism) is unverified — the verification that would remove it is longitudinal employer/graduate-outcome survey data, which does not yet exist for this policy change.

### Conclusion C3: The naive full switch to unverified take-home assessment (option B, the literal reading of the policy question) is not viable for any course making an individual-capability claim

## What the question is actually asking

Stripped of its binary framing, the real question is: **given that AI can now perform much of the cognitive work an assessment elicits, undetectably in most cases, which assessment format(s) — not necessarily either of the two named — actually support the credentialing and learning-feedback inferences a given course needs to certify, at a resourcing and equity cost the institution can sustain?**

That reframing matters because "timed exam vs. take-home" is a false binary, and treating it as the whole decision space is itself the first thing worth discarding.

## Assumptions worth challenging in the framing

- **"It's binary."** False — task redesign, verification steps, and construct redefinition are independent levers, not just "which of two formats." At least four viable options exist besides the status quo.
- **"AI-assisted writing is inherently illegitimate."** Only true relative to a specific construct being certified. If the course's stated goal is "can this person produce good judgment using available tools," AI use isn't cheating — it's the tool the credential should certify competence *with*.
- **"The pre-AI exam was a clean baseline AI is now corrupting."** False. Timed, proctored exams have long carried *construct-irrelevant variance* — score differences driven by speededness and induced stress rather than the actual target skill (this is a named problem in the assessment-validity literature going back to Messick, 1989). AI didn't break a clean measure; it removed the one thing (resistance to undetectable outside help) that was propping up an already-imperfect format.
- **"Detection is the only lever."** Also false, and importantly so: tested AI-detectors carry a severe, *biased* false-positive rate — one peer-reviewed study found 61% false positives on non-native-English writing vs. 5% on native writing, with 98% of non-native essays flagged by at least one detector. Any policy leaning on detector output as a primary integrity mechanism imports a discrimination problem into the fix. This should be ruled out categorically regardless of which format wins.
- **"A university-wide blanket policy is the right unit of decision."** Not obviously — the correct grain is closer to *the course*, since different courses certify different constructs.

## The core trade-off

An unverified take-home artifact is, by a basic fact about text as a medium, indistinguishable from an AI-generated one for most open-ended writing prompts — no inspection of the finished product reveals *how* it was produced. So a **naive full switch to unverified take-home work fails outright** for any course making an individual-capability claim. It only survives for assessments that don't claim to certify individual capability at all (e.g., explicitly AI-collaborative team deliverables).

That leaves four real contenders, scored against six weighted criteria (construct validity, AI-substitution resistance, equity, resource feasibility, field-relative authenticity, student wellbeing):

| | Status quo (timed/proctored) | Authentic take-home + verification (oral check, etc.) | AI-inclusive timed judgment task | Portfolio + periodic checks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weighted score (of 105) | 66 | 76 | **78** | 74 |

The status quo comes in clearly last for any course whose target construct isn't itself unaided real-time performance. The top two are a near-tie — sensitive to how much an institution weights student wellbeing versus integrity — so this isn't a landslide result, it's a genuine judgment call at the margin.

## Conclusion

Not a flat yes or no. The construct-appropriate answer differs by course:

- **Where the real-world task is AI-saturated professional judgment** (most knowledge work): move to timed, proctored, *AI-inclusive* assessments — critique, correct, or extend an AI-generated draft under time pressure. This directly tests the actual post-graduation skill rather than unaided recall, and reuses existing proctoring infrastructure.
- **Where the target is applied synthesis without a hard real-time requirement**: authentic take-home work (using inputs a generic AI session can't access — course-specific data, in-class artifacts) paired with a standardized, accommodation-built-in verification step (a brief oral check, process/draft tracking), or a portfolio model where resourcing supports it.
- **Where the downstream task genuinely requires unaided real-time performance** (licensure boards, emergency medicine, courtroom advocacy, live interpretation): keep the timed, proctored, closed exam — this is the identifiable minority case where the status quo is still correct.
- **Never**: adopt AI-detection software as the primary integrity mechanism, given its documented discriminatory false-positive profile.

**Why confidence is low rather than high, honestly stated:** two load-bearing claims are unverified against real institutional data — (1) that verification/authenticity steps actually close the authorship-ambiguity gap in practice rather than just adding friction, and (2) that institutions will actually fund the redesign (protected faculty time, standardized oral-check protocols, TA support) rather than doing it cosmetically. A pre-mortem on an 18-month rollout surfaces a plausible failure mode worth naming explicitly: redesign done without resourcing degrades into relabeled old assignments with an inconsistently-applied oral check that itself creates a new equity complaint (live-speech performance bias replacing text-detector bias), while employers who were never told the credential's meaning changed lose trust when it surfaces years later. None of that invalidates the conclusion — it just means the answer is contingent on a resourced, accommodated, externally-communicated pilot, not a policy memo. If a university can't or won't fund that, the honest fallback is closer to the status quo than to a naive take-home switch.

Stripped of its binary framing, the real question is: **given that AI can now perform much of the cognitive work an assessment elicits, undetectably in most cases, which assessment format(s) — not necessarily either of the two named — actually support the credentialing and learning-feedback inferences a given course needs to certify, at a resourcing and equity cost the institution can sustain?**

That reframing matters because "timed exam vs. take-home" is a false binary, and treating it as the whole decision space is itself the first thing worth discarding.

## Assumptions worth challenging in the framing

- **"It's binary."** False — task redesign, verification steps, and construct redefinition are independent levers, not just "which of two formats." At least four viable options exist besides the status quo.
- **"AI-assisted writing is inherently illegitimate."** Only true relative to a specific construct being certified. If the course's stated goal is "can this person produce good judgment using available tools," AI use isn't cheating — it's the tool the credential should certify competence *with*.
- **"The pre-AI exam was a clean baseline AI is now corrupting."** False. Timed, proctored exams have long carried *construct-irrelevant variance* — score differences driven by speededness and induced stress rather than the actual target skill (this is a named problem in the assessment-validity literature going back to Messick, 1989). AI didn't break a clean measure; it removed the one thing (resistance to undetectable outside help) that was propping up an already-imperfect format.
- **"Detection is the only lever."** Also false, and importantly so: tested AI-detectors carry a severe, *biased* false-positive rate — one peer-reviewed study found 61% false positives on non-native-English writing vs. 5% on native writing, with 98% of non-native essays flagged by at least one detector. Any policy leaning on detector output as a primary integrity mechanism imports a discrimination problem into the fix. This should be ruled out categorically regardless of which format wins.
- **"A university-wide blanket policy is the right unit of decision."** Not obviously — the correct grain is closer to *the course*, since different courses certify different constructs.

## The core trade-off

An unverified take-home artifact is, by a basic fact about text as a medium, indistinguishable from an AI-generated one for most open-ended writing prompts — no inspection of the finished product reveals *how* it was produced. So a **naive full switch to unverified take-home work fails outright** for any course making an individual-capability claim. It only survives for assessments that don't claim to certify individual capability at all (e.g., explicitly AI-collaborative team deliverables).

That leaves four real contenders, scored against six weighted criteria (construct validity, AI-substitution resistance, equity, resource feasibility, field-relative authenticity, student wellbeing):

| | Status quo (timed/proctored) | Authentic take-home + verification (oral check, etc.) | AI-inclusive timed judgment task | Portfolio + periodic checks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weighted score (of 105) | 66 | 76 | **78** | 74 |

The status quo comes in clearly last for any course whose target construct isn't itself unaided real-time performance. The top two are a near-tie — sensitive to how much an institution weights student wellbeing versus integrity — so this isn't a landslide result, it's a genuine judgment call at the margin.

## Conclusion

Not a flat yes or no. The construct-appropriate answer differs by course:

- **Where the real-world task is AI-saturated professional judgment** (most knowledge work): move to timed, proctored, *AI-inclusive* assessments — critique, correct, or extend an AI-generated draft under time pressure. This directly tests the actual post-graduation skill rather than unaided recall, and reuses existing proctoring infrastructure.
- **Where the target is applied synthesis without a hard real-time requirement**: authentic take-home work (using inputs a generic AI session can't access — course-specific data, in-class artifacts) paired with a standardized, accommodation-built-in verification step (a brief oral check, process/draft tracking), or a portfolio model where resourcing supports it.
- **Where the downstream task genuinely requires unaided real-time performance** (licensure boards, emergency medicine, courtroom advocacy, live interpretation): keep the timed, proctored, closed exam — this is the identifiable minority case where the status quo is still correct.
- **Never**: adopt AI-detection software as the primary integrity mechanism, given its documented discriminatory false-positive profile.

**Why confidence is low rather than high, honestly stated:** two load-bearing claims are unverified against real institutional data — (1) that verification/authenticity steps actually close the authorship-ambiguity gap in practice rather than just adding friction, and (2) that institutions will actually fund the redesign (protected faculty time, standardized oral-check protocols, TA support) rather than doing it cosmetically. A pre-mortem on an 18-month rollout surfaces a plausible failure mode worth naming explicitly: redesign done without resourcing degrades into relabeled old assignments with an inconsistently-applied oral check that itself creates a new equity complaint (live-speech performance bias replacing text-detector bias), while employers who were never told the credential's meaning changed lose trust when it surfaces years later. None of that invalidates the conclusion — it just means the answer is contingent on a resourced, accommodated, externally-communicated pilot, not a policy memo. If a university can't or won't fund that, the honest fallback is closer to the status quo than to a naive take-home switch.
